Continuous performance surveillance is mandatory under the FDA’s AI/ML SaMD framework. Under the Food and Drug Administration’s regulatory framework, an AI‑based clinical decision support (CDS) tool that influences diagnosis or treatment is treated as a medical device if it meets the definition of “software that performs one or more functions that are intended to be used for the purpose of diagnosing, curing, mitigating, treating, or preventing disease.” The FDA’s 2023 guidance on SaMD risk‑based classification (the *SaMD Regulatory Framework* and the *Risk Management Guidance*) requires a health system to first determine whether the tool is “high‑risk” (Class II or III) or “low‑risk” (Class I). While HIPAA establishes a federal baseline for protected health information (PHI), many states have enacted stricter privacy statutes that apply to any entity handling personal data, including AI vendors. The California Consumer Privacy Act (CPRA) now imposes obligations on “data fiduciaries” that process consumer data, requiring explicit notice of data use, the right to opt‑out of automated decision‑making, and rigorous data minimization practices. New York’s SHIELD Act extends privacy protections to non‑PHI personal information and mandates breach notification within 30 days. Because state laws differ, a jurisdiction‑specific compliance matrix is essential; failure to honor a single state’s opt‑out right can trigger civil penalties ranging from $1,000 per violation under CPRA to statutory damages under the New York SHIELD Act.
